title: Correlation in levels vs in returns — Pearson and Spearman

explain.prompt: Compare the reports for Brent–WTI and Brent–coffee. In 4–6 sentences: why is the coffee–Brent correlation 0.77 in levels but ≈ 0.03 in returns? Which of the two numbers measures a link? Why can a high correlation of daily returns between Brent and WTI still not tell you which market drives the other?
rubric: Coffee and Brent are independent by construction; their level correlation (≈ 0.77) comes from two trending, non-stationary paths that happened to drift the same way — a spurious correlation.
Correlation of returns (≈ 0.03) measures whether the two prices move together day by day; it is the meaningful number. Rule: correlate changes, not non-stationary levels.
Brent–WTI: high in both (0.99 levels, 0.88 returns) — consistent with a real link, but the level figure on its own proves nothing.
Pearson measures linear dependence and is sensitive to extreme days; Spearman works on ranks (monotone dependence, robust to outliers) — here they agree (0.88 vs 0.86).
Correlation ≠ causality: a common factor (the global crude balance) drives both; correlation is symmetric and says nothing about direction or about what happens if one price is pushed.
With dependent observations the effective sample size is smaller than n, so the usual significance levels of correlations are too optimistic.
